title: Signs Your Deck Needs Repair Before It Becomes a Safety Hazard
seoTitle: Deck Repair Warning Signs: Fix It Before It's Unsafe
seoDescription: Soft boards, loose railings, ledger board problems and corroded hardware: how to spot a deck that needs repair before it becomes a hazard.
html:
Deck failures are more common than most homeowners realize, and they rarely happen with warning. The problem is that structural decay happens out of sight — in the ledger board connection, the post bases, and the beam-to-joist connections. By the time a deck looks problematic, it may already be a serious safety hazard. Seasonal maintenance is the most effective way to catch problems early rather than after they've compounded.

Soft or Spongy Boards

Walk the entire deck surface slowly. Any boards that feel soft or give underfoot have moisture-compromised wood fibres and need to be replaced. Pay special attention to boards near the house, around post penetrations, and anywhere water tends to pool. Don't just replace the surface boards — probe the joists below before putting new decking over rotten framing.

Loose Railing and Wobbly Posts

Give every railing section a firm lateral push. In Ontario, the building code requires deck railings to resist significant lateral load — roughly the weight of a person falling against it. Any railing that moves perceptibly under hand pressure is not meeting this requirement. Post bases that are buried in the ground or sitting in standing water are a common failure point.

The Ledger Board Connection

The ledger board — where the deck attaches to the house — is the most critical connection and the most common failure point. Water wicks between the ledger and the house wall, promoting rot in both the ledger and the rim joist of the house. Check for staining, paint peeling, or soft wood along this connection. If there's any flexibility when you push on the deck near the house, investigate immediately.

Proper ledger connections use lag bolts at specific spacing intervals, with flashing above to direct water away from the joint. Many older decks were built with nailed ledgers, which is no longer code-compliant and significantly increases failure risk. If you're opening a cottage in spring, the ledger connection is one of the critical items to check during your walkthrough.

Corroded Hardware

Steel fasteners, joist hangers, post bases, and connectors corrode over time — especially in the treated lumber environment. Red rust staining on wood surfaces is a sign that hardware is failing. Heavily corroded joist hangers can lose most of their rated capacity while still looking like they're holding. When inspecting or repairing a deck, replace all compromised hardware, not just the visible fasteners.
